tagline.text: Philosophy that starts from the single person who must choose how to live.

overview.text: Existentialism is a loose family of ideas, not a tidy school. It starts from life as a person lives it, not from a detached viewpoint. One of its core ideas is that we make ourselves through our choices, and we are responsible for who we become. Two nineteenth-century thinkers laid the groundwork: Søren Kierkegaard, from Denmark, and the German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche. It became famous in mid-twentieth-century France through Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir, two French philosophers who also wrote novels.

overview.text: It rejects fixed moral rules, but it does not say that morality is empty. A good life is still possible: one where we own our choices and help others be free too.

themes.title: Existence before essence
themes.summary: Your choices shape who you become, within real limits.

paragraphs.text: Sartre called it 'the first principle of existentialism': existence precedes essence. Your 'essence' would be a fixed nature that decides who you are. Existentialists say we are not born with one. A person first 'turns up' and only afterwards defines himself, through choices made as life unfolds. Sartre adapted the idea from the German philosopher Martin Heidegger. Hard facts still limit us, such as our body and the time and place we live in. But we can question those facts, give them meaning and decide what to do with them. A strong craving, for example, does not force me to act on it.

sources.quote: the first principle of existentialism
not as a substance or thing with some pre-given nature
twentieth-century German philosophers like Edmund Husserl, Martin Heidegger, and Karl Jaspers
I do not out of necessity have to act on these desires

themes.title: Freedom and anxiety
themes.summary: No one else can make your choices for you, and that can feel dizzying.

paragraphs.text: This makes us free, and responsible for what we make of ourselves. Take Sartre's example of a coward. Childhood or genes did not make him that way; he 'makes himself a coward' by his decisions. No god and no absolute moral rule can choose for us or excuse us. Realising this brings anxiety. Kierkegaard called anxiety 'the dizziness of freedom'. Existentialists ask us to face this feeling, not run from it. It can shake us out of our comfortable routines.

themes.title: Authenticity versus the crowd
themes.summary: Going along with everyone feels comforting, but it lets us dodge our own choices.

paragraphs.text: Being authentic means being true to yourself. Existentialists criticise our habit of living by the rules and expectations of everyone around us. Heidegger's name for this crowd was 'the They'. We enjoy, read and judge things as 'they' do. It feels like living well, but it hides our freedom from us. So we are deceiving ourselves. Sartre and Beauvoir call this self-deception 'bad faith'. It comes in two forms:

themes.title: Meaning without guarantees
themes.summary: Without God or a built-in purpose, meaning has to be made, not found.

paragraphs.text: As nineteenth-century Europe became less religious and more scientific, the old religious picture that gave life moral direction began to collapse. Nietzsche diagnosed the result: nihilism, the shocking sense that our existence has no overall reason or purpose. His image for this loss was 'the death of God'. The French novelist Albert Camus called our situation 'the absurd'. It is the clash between our 'wild longing for clarity' and 'the unreasonable silence of the world'. Camus asked whether such a life is worth living. His answer was yes: the absurd calls for action, not suicide. Beauvoir insisted that existence is not absurd but 'ambiguous'. Calling it absurd, she said, denies that it can ever be given a meaning. Calling it ambiguous says 'its meaning is never fixed', so we keep making it.

themes.title: My freedom needs yours
themes.summary: Other people can trap us as objects, yet my freedom depends on theirs.

paragraphs.text: Sartre and Beauvoir argued that we see ourselves through 'the look' of others. Their gaze can turn us into objects. Relationships then become a power struggle. Sartre's play No Exit sums this up in its famous line that hell is other people. But there is a better way. Beauvoir's 'authentic love' nurtures the other person's freedom instead of possessing them. Why does my freedom need yours? If I value my own freedom, I must also want it for others. As Sartre put it, in wanting freedom 'we discover that it depends entirely on the freedom of others'.

sources.quote: Hell is—other people
depends entirely on the freedom of others

themes.title: Faith and the leap
themes.summary: For religious existentialists, faith is a personal commitment reason can't justify.

paragraphs.text: Existentialism is not only atheist. Kierkegaard was a Christian. He prized 'a truth which is true for me', lived and felt rather than proved. His book Fear and Trembling retells the Bible story in which God tells Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. Here is the paradox. As a father, Abraham has a moral duty to protect his son. God's command asks him to break that duty. By committing to God's command, Abraham becomes a 'knight of faith': someone who puts a personal truth above ordinary morality, a truth reason cannot make sense of. Nietzsche and Sartre, by contrast, saw God as irrelevant or even harmful to our deepest choices.

sources.quote: a truth which is true for me

paragraphs.text: The label 'existentialist' is itself disputed. Of the major figures, only Sartre and Beauvoir openly claimed it. Heidegger and Camus both rejected it. Even so, scholars still place both within the tradition. Some argue the label does more harm than good, because it lumps very different ideas together.

thinkers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
thinkers.summary: Søren Kierkegaard was born in Copenhagen in 1813 and wrote mostly in the 1840s, across philosophy, theology, psychology and social critique. He opposed building grand systems and is often called the 'father of existentialism', though SEP warns the label hides as much as it shows. He has often been cast as Hegel's great opponent, but recent scholars think his main target was certain Danish Hegelians.

key_ideas.text: A self is not something you simply have but something you must become, by holding together what is given and what is possible.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
thinkers.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and cultural critic who published intensively in the 1870s and 1880s. He is famous for fierce attacks on traditional European morality and religion, often by exposing the hidden psychology behind received ideas. He also proposed new values he hoped would renew culture, and SEP's existentialism entry counts him among the movement's nineteenth-century pioneers.

key_ideas.text: 'God is dead': belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable, so the morality built on it is set to collapse.
Imagine living your life over and over forever; on one influential reading, your reaction tests how much you value your life (eternal recurrence).

thinkers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
thinkers.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre was, with Simone de Beauvoir, the most popular voice of mid-twentieth-century French existentialism, and a novelist, playwright and public intellectual. His treatise Being and Nothingness (1943) is called the defining work of the movement, and his 1945 lecture Existentialism is a Humanism drew huge crowds. Later he tried to combine existentialism with Marxism.

key_ideas.text: Existence precedes essence: we turn up first and define ourselves afterward through our choices.
We are 'condemned' to be free: no fact about our situation fixes how we respond to it, so we are responsible.
Bad faith is self-deception: denying either our freedom or the facts of our situation.

thinkers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
thinkers.summary: Simone de Beauvoir was a philosopher, novelist, feminist and activist, and one of the major figures of post-war French existentialism. She is best known for The Second Sex (1949), her trailblazing work in feminist philosophy. She called herself an author rather than a philosopher, but scholarship has secured her place as a thinker in her own right, not merely Sartre's helper.

thinkers.name: Albert Camus
thinkers.summary: Albert Camus was a journalist, novelist, playwright and essayist who more than once denied being a philosopher. His Myth of Sisyphus sits squarely in the existentialist tradition, yet he denied being an existentialist and wrote against Kierkegaard, Jaspers and Heidegger. He won the Nobel Prize for literature in 1957 and died in a car accident in 1960.

intro.text: Existentialist ideas shaped existential psychotherapy, which helps people with questions such as meaning and the fear of death. One example is logotherapy, a therapy built around finding meaning. It was created by the Austrian psychiatrist Viktor Frankl.

sources.quote: the Austrian Frankl, who invented the method of logotherapy
to help clients address such issues in their lives as meaning and death anxiety

practices.title: Notice who you chose to ask

idea.text: As we saw, no god or moral law can choose for us. Sartre put it starkly: 'there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us'.

sources.quote: there are no excuses behind us nor justifications before us

practices.from: Jean-Paul Sartre, Existentialism is a Humanism

practice.text: Sartre's own example is a student of his in wartime France. He could go to England and fight with the Free French Forces. Or he could stay with his mother, who lived only for him. He came to Sartre for advice. But choosing an adviser, Sartre said, is already a choice: you more or less know what they will say. His only reply was 'You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent.' One way to use his point: before your next hard choice, ask yourself why you picked the person you are asking, and what you already expect them to say.

sources.quote: to choose an adviser is nevertheless to commit oneself by that choice
You are free, therefore choose, that is to say, invent
the choice between going to England to join the Free French Forces or of staying near his mother

practices.title: Ask what this moment asks of you

idea.text: On meaning, Frankl disagrees with Sartre and Beauvoir. They hold that we make meaning through our choices. Frankl holds that meaning exists for us to discover, and that we cannot make it. A 2015 review of existential therapy trials found that meaning-focused therapy strengthened people's sense of meaning, but the studies were few and low in quality, and they tested therapy, not reflecting alone.

practice.text: Frankl also turned the usual question round. We should not ask what life means, he said: 'each man is questioned by life'. We answer by taking responsibility for our own life. Logotherapists often guide people by asking questions, so that they find meanings for themselves. Frankl named three avenues to meaning. One way to borrow that on your own: this week, ask yourself how each avenue showed up for you.

idea.text: As we saw, Nietzsche's ideal was saying yes to your whole life, the good and the bad. He called this attitude amor fati: love of one's fate. He thought only 'the highest types' could truly live this way. You do not have to share his elitism to try his question.

sources.quote: The key to living with style is, for Nietzsche, a radical acceptance
the highest types

practice.text: Imagine a demon tells you that you must live this life again, 'innumerable times', with nothing new in it. Would you curse the demon? Or would you answer that you never heard anything more divine? If the thought took hold of you, Nietzsche wrote, it would transform you, or perhaps crush you. One influential reading treats it as a test of whether your life has been good, as a whole and in every detail. If that feels too big, one way in (our adaptation, not his): ask it of a single day first.

sources.quote: If that thought acquired power over thee, as thou art, it would transform thee, and perhaps crush thee
